title: The Many Layers of NGC 1808
caption: The barred spiral galaxy NGC 1808, imaged by the Dark Energy Camera on the Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope
celestial: NGC 1808 · constellation Columba · about 40 million light-years away (source figure)
credit: Dark Energy Survey/DOE/FNAL/DECam/CTIO/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA. Image processing: R. Colombari and M. Zamani (NSF NOIRLab)

recognition.text: NOIRLab Image of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: A faint blue ring encircles the smouldering centre of NGC 1808, a barred spiral galaxy in the southern constellation Columba, the Dove. Dark dust lanes lace through the galaxy's middle region, and softly glowing outer arms, slightly warped, surround it all.

The core is thought to host a supermassive black hole, marked by material falling onto it and unusually high brightness. The ring around it holds star clusters and supernova remnants and is a site of starburst activity, where an exceptional number of hot, bright young stars are being produced. The dust lanes are the result of large outflows of hydrogen gas from the nucleus.

This burst of star formation is thought to stem from tidal encounters in the past with NGC 1792, a nearby galaxy. The warped outer arms point the same way, since such an encounter could have given NGC 1808 its lopsided shape and driven gas toward the nucleus, igniting star formation in its ring.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (19.38 x 10.90 arcminutes) and distance (40 million light years), the frame spans roughly 225,000 × 127,000 light-years. Its light set out about 40 million years before reaching the telescope.
